record.paper_title: Quantum Communication: From Fundamentals to Recent Trends, Challenges and Open Problems
record.original_question: How can multiqubit quantum network nodes realize robust and highly efficient conversion interfaces with high signal-to-noise ratio, including interfaces that connect microwave-domain quantum processors such as superconducting qubit circuits to optical communication carriers?

evidence.quote: Integrating multiple robust memories into a multiqubit network node could bring us closer to achieving the highest stages of the quantum internet. However, a key challenge lies in realizing a robust and highly efficient converter with a high signal-to-noise ratio.

Alternatively, end nodes could consist of a quantum processor with qubit frequencies in the microwave domain, such as a superconducting qubit circuit, paired with a microwave-to-optical conversion process.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider a quantum network whose end nodes are multiqubit registers, and in particular nodes consisting of a superconducting qubit processor whose qubit transition frequencies lie in the microwave regime (a few GHz), connected via optical-frequency photonic channels (hundreds of THz) used as long-distance flying-qubit carriers. A quantum conversion interface between such a node and the optical channel is modeled as a completely positive trace-preserving map (a quantum channel) Φ that coherently maps the state of an itinerant microwave photonic mode to an itinerant optical photonic mode (and vice versa), characterized by:
 (i) a conversion efficiency η ∈ [0,1], defined as the probability that a single input photon is transferred to the output mode;
 (ii) an added-noise figure n̄ (in units of photons referred to the input), with the corresponding signal-to-noise ratio for a single-photon input given by SNR = η/(η + 2 n̄ + …) in the high-SNR regime;
 (iii) a bandwidth B, fidelity F with respect to the identity channel on a chosen qubit encoding, and robustness to environmental fluctuations and integration into a multiqubit node.

Problem. Devise an explicit physical model and an associated quantum channel Φ implementing such a microwave-to-optical (and optical-to-microwave) conversion interface, suitable for integration with multiqubit network nodes, that simultaneously achieves:
 • near-unit conversion efficiency η → 1,
 • vanishingly small added noise n̄ → 0 (so that the high-SNR limit is reached),
 • high process fidelity F preserving entanglement of the transferred qubits,
 • robustness against realistic loss, thermal occupation, and parameter drift,
while remaining compatible with multiqubit superconducting processors. Equivalently, identify fundamental upper bounds on the achievable (η, n̄, F, B) tuple for any physically realizable bidirectional microwave–optical quantum transducer, and exhibit a construction approaching these bounds.
artifact.status_search_result: Microwave-to-optical quantum transduction with simultaneously high efficiency, low added noise, and high bandwidth remains an active and unresolved research problem. Recent (2023–2025) experimental demonstrations using electro-optic, piezo-optomechanical, and magnonic platforms report efficiencies typically well below unity and added noise above the quantum-limited threshold; surveys describe achieving quantum-enabled, high-SNR transducers integrated with multiqubit superconducting nodes as an outstanding open challenge.

status_evidence.title: Perspectives on quantum transduction (Lauk et al., updated reviews)
status_evidence.snippet: Reviews microwave-to-optical transduction approaches and lists efficiency–noise–bandwidth trade-offs as open challenges.
status_evidence.claim: Achieving simultaneously high efficiency and low added noise in microwave-to-optical quantum transducers is an open problem.

status_evidence.title: Recent progress on microwave-to-optical quantum transduction
status_evidence.snippet: Surveys 2023–2024 platforms (electro-optic, optomechanical, magnonic, atomic) and notes that no platform has yet reached the high-efficiency, near-quantum-limited noise regime required for fault-tolerant quantum networking.
status_evidence.claim: As of 2024, no transducer has achieved the combined high-efficiency, low-noise, high-bandwidth regime needed for robust quantum networking with superconducting nodes.
